clue.text: Company business comes before a drink

indicators.note: 'comes before' is an instruction about order: the pieces named so far are written first and what follows them goes on the end.

parts.note: co. is the everyday short form of company
a business is a company too, so co. does duty a second time
the clue's own indefinite article, taken as a single letter

explanation.surface: Work gets dealt with first and the drink is the reward waiting at the end of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Two different words hand over the same two letters: 'company' and 'business' are both co., and doubling a piece like that is what makes the wordplay look too thin to be right.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is the hot chocolate made from the powder, so 'drink' is the plainest sort of synonym: the noun for what ends up in the mug.

clue.text: Make a mess of power grab acquiring fashion brand

indicators.note: 'acquiring' is a taking-in word: whatever acquires something wraps round it and holds it inside rather than beside it.

parts.note: a coup is a seizure of power
CK is Calvin Klein, the label's two initials as stamped on the clothing

explanation.surface: A grab for power goes wrong, and the plotters end up buying a designer label.
explanation.walkthrough: A designer's initials are standard crossword currency, and the surface never admits that clothing is involved — 'fashion brand' looks like the thing being seized.
explanation.definitionFit: To cock something up is British slang for botching it, so the phrasal verb answers 'make a mess of' exactly, tense for tense.

clue.text: Devoted Christian's two chapters about ancient city soldier …

indicators.note: 'about' puts one piece around another: to be about something is to be all round the outside of it.

parts.note: chapter is abbreviated ch., and the clue asks for a pair of them
Ur was the Sumerian city of the Old Testament, and the crossword's usual ancient city
a man is a soldier of the ranks, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: A devout author's two chapters describe a soldier from an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing dots hand the sentence on to 3 down and carry no letters with them: the two clues share a picture, not a mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: A churchman is a clergyman, or any committed member of the church, which is what 'devoted Christian' names — singular noun for singular noun.

clue.text: … partially mislead her enthusiastic follower

indicators.note: 'partially' says only part of the words is wanted, which is the standard flag for a run of letters lying inside them.

parts.note: the letters run consecutively across the three words, beginning inside the first of them

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic follower is being partly misled by the person she looks up to.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry the sentence over from 2 down, which is why the eye reads 'mislead her' as ordinary phrasing and never stops there to count letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An adherent is someone who sticks to a leader or a cause, so 'follower' is a direct synonym — same singular noun, same sense of allegiance.

clue.text: Reggie's finally tired of cooked breakfast?

definitions.note: The answer is plural and 'breakfast' is not: the setter is naming the meal by the thing on the plate, which is what the question mark admits to.

indicators.note: 'finally' asks for last letters only, so the words after it give up nothing except the letter each one ends on.
'cooked' is a change-of-state word: what comes out of the pan no longer looks like what went in, letters included.

parts.note: the name's seven letters, apostrophe and all, are the bulk of the fodder
the closing letters of these two words, in the order they stand

explanation.surface: Reggie has at last gone off the greasy breakfast he used to look forward to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' reaches across both 'tired' and 'of', which is the step that hides: one small indicator harvesting the last letter of two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: Fried eggs are the defining item of a British cooked breakfast, so the definition works by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Basic for baptism that rector's in prominent position

indicators.note: 'in' is the plain container word: the rector is put inside the other piece rather than added onto the end of it.

parts.note: the font is the stone basin a church keeps its baptismal water in
R is the standard short form of rector on a parish noticeboard

explanation.surface: The essentials of a christening, with the rector standing where the whole congregation can see him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basic for baptism' is a church fitting rather than anything doctrinal, and a solver hunting for water or faith loses time before the stone basin arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: The front is the prominent position — the head of a queue, a procession or a stage, the place where you are most visible.

clue.text: Tablet dad found amongst papers

indicators.note: 'found amongst' is a container instruction: one piece turns up in the middle of another instead of next to it.

parts.note: your papers are your identity documents — ID
pa is the familiar word for a father

explanation.surface: Dad has been found somewhere in a heap of paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tablet' is the gadget, not the pill or the stone tablet of the commandments — Coot leans on the newest of the word's three senses while the surface stays in the filing cabinet.
explanation.definitionFit: An iPad is the best-known tablet computer, so the definition names the category and the answer supplies the brand that stands for it.

clue.text: Over for a day, walk in the park and draw (nothing in particular)

indicators.note: 'for' is the swap word here: one letter is written where the other used to be, rather than joined onto it.

parts.note: a doddle is something that takes no effort at all
O is the over on a cricket scorecard, and it is the letter moving in
d is the standard short form of day, and it is the letter giving up its place

explanation.surface: A visitor over for the day takes a stroll through the park and sketches whatever is in front of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk in the park' is the idiom for something easy rather than an actual stroll, which is exactly what the surface's park is there to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: To doodle is to draw aimlessly, and 'nothing in particular' is the setter spelling out that the drawing has no subject.

clue.text: Remarkable rasping sound heard

indicators.note: A 'sound heard' points at pronunciation rather than spelling, so you write the version that fits the grid, not the one the clue's word uses.

parts.note: to rasp is to grate, and said aloud that word has a second spelling

explanation.surface: Somebody has picked up a harsh scraping noise and thinks it is impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words spelled quite differently share one pronunciation, and the clue gives you the harsh one to lead you away from the flattering one.
explanation.definitionFit: Great means remarkable in the everyday sense of standing out — a great performance is one worth remarking on.

clue.text: Eric and Ernie wanted this star to excel

parts.note: the sun is the star our own sky has
to shine at something is to excel at it

explanation.surface: Eric and Ernie are hoping the celebrity booked for the show will be brilliant on the night.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise were Britain's biggest television double act, and they closed every programme singing the request the definition quotes.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Bring Me Sunshine' was Morecambe and Wise's signing-off song, so what Eric and Ernie wanted is the weather named in its title.

clue.text: Lazybones put across rubbish business cases

parts.note: to couch something is to put it across in words of a particular kind

indicators.note: 'cases' is a verb here: to case something is to enclose it, so the piece it names shuts around another.

parts.note: business is the nursery euphemism, as in doing one's business, and it opens up to take something in
tat is cheap rubbishy stuff

explanation.surface: The idler of the office is presenting weak business cases and convincing nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business cases' looks like the phrase the surface needs, and it is two separate instructions: a euphemism for what the dog left, and a verb meaning to enclose.
explanation.definitionFit: A couch potato is someone who lies about watching television, which is what 'lazybones' names — an idler, said with the same affection.

clue.text: Heroin taken regularly for a long time

indicators.note: 'taken regularly' means at a fixed interval, and the interval here is every second letter rather than every letter.

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word, read in order

explanation.surface: Someone has been taking the drug steadily for years on end.
explanation.walkthrough: Alternate letters usually start at the first one; the count here begins at the second, which is why the source word looks two letters too long to fit.
explanation.definitionFit: An eon is an immense stretch of time, the geologist's unit, so 'a long time' is the everyday phrase for that noun.

clue.text: Rotten clues mostly deserve to fester?

indicators.note: 'Rotten' describes something decayed and out of shape, and letters in a rotten word no longer sit where they started.
'mostly' means take most of a word — all of it except the letter it ends on.

parts.note: the plural loses its final letter before anything is shuffled
to rate a mention is to deserve one

explanation.surface: Bad clues deserve to rot away, which is a setter making a joke at his own expense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten' looks like a verdict on the clues and is the instruction instead, and Coot is happy to let the insult land on his own puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: To ulcerate is to break down into an open sore that will not heal, and 'fester' is the everyday verb for the same suppuration.

clue.text: Irregular discoloration left within clumsy work

indicators.note: 'within' puts the letter it follows inside the word that comes next, dropping it into the middle rather than onto an end.

parts.note: a botch is a clumsily made job
L is the standard short form of left

explanation.surface: A patch of uneven colour is what the careless workmanship has left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is a letter, not the past tense the sentence wants — the surface reads it as what the work left behind, and that is where the parse stalls.
explanation.definitionFit: A blotch is a patch of colour that has spread unevenly across skin or fabric, which is irregular discoloration in dictionary terms.

clue.text: Some recalled you as extremely hairy man

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of the words that follow rather than all of them, the usual flag for letters already lying in the clue.
'recalled' means called back, so the run of letters is read in the opposite direction to the way it is printed.

parts.note: the letters run backwards across the word breaks, starting inside the last of the three

explanation.surface: Old acquaintances remember you as having been extraordinarily hairy.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau in Genesis was born covered in hair, which is how his brother Jacob was able to fool their blind father with a goatskin on his arms.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau, Isaac's elder son, is described in Genesis as red and hairy all over, so the definition identifies him by his one famous feature.

clue.text: Stokes close to speechless defending home record

definitions.note: 'Record' is singular and the answer is not: the minutes of a meeting are one record made of many entries, and the word has no singular in that sense.

indicators.note: 'close to' is a placement instruction: the letter it names is written up against the rest of the assembly, not inside it.
'defending' is a surrounding word — whatever defends something stands all round the outside of it.

parts.note: someone mute has no speech
to be in is to be at home
the stokes, the unit of kinematic viscosity, is written S

explanation.surface: A cricketer, nearly lost for words, is defending his side's unbeaten home record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stokes' is the surface's England all-rounder and the wordplay's unit of viscosity, named after the physicist George Stokes — one letter hiding behind a famous name.
explanation.definitionFit: The minutes are the written record of what was said and decided at a meeting, kept by the secretary.

clue.text: Getting sides confused, presenter is rubbish

indicators.note: The 'sides' are the outer letters and 'confused' muddles them, so the two ends of the word change places.

parts.note: the host is the one presenting the show

explanation.surface: The commentator keeps mixing up the two teams and is useless at his job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sides' means teams in the surface and outer letters in the wordplay, and only those two letters move — everything between them stays put.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosh is British slang for nonsense, the sense of 'rubbish' that means talk not worth listening to rather than refuse.

clue.text: Sir Elton abandons husband in favour of American woman

indicators.note: 'abandons' is the losing half of the swap: the letter named next is dropped and does not appear.
'in favour of' names the replacement — the thing preferred takes the seat that has just been emptied.

parts.note: Sir Elton John, the knighted British singer, supplies his surname
H is the standard short form of husband, and it is the letter being dropped
A is the standard short form of American, and it is the letter moving in

explanation.surface: Elton drops his husband and takes up with an American woman instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Elton has a husband in real life, which is what gives the surface its sting; the wordplay only ever wanted his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan is a woman's name, so the definition works by example: a given name is defined by the category it belongs to.

clue.text: See lover agitated — terminal to relationship to miss alarm?

indicators.note: Something agitated is shaken about, and letters shaken about do not come to rest where they began.
'terminal' names the end of a thing, so only the last letter of the word after it is taken.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, both words taken whole
the letter this word ends on

explanation.surface: An agitated lover, at the end of the affair, is in no state to hear the morning alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'terminal to relationship' read as the end of the affair, which is the surface talking while the words do plain letter-picking underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversleep is to sleep past the hour you meant to wake, which is what missing your alarm comes to — the question mark flags the loose phrasing.

clue.text: Cringe at awful food at function

indicators.note: 'awful' is a spoiling word: food called awful has been turned into something other than what it should have been, and so have the letters.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, exactly the length of the entry

explanation.surface: The buffet at the reception is bad enough to make the guests wince.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' appears twice and only the first one belongs to the fodder; the eye slides between them, which is what hides where the definition starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Catering is the trade of supplying food for an event, so the definition describes the job rather than offering a one-word synonym.

clue.text: Turned up anxious for culinary courses

indicators.note: 'Turned up' is a reversal on a down entry: the letters are read from the bottom of the column upwards.

parts.note: anxious gives STRESSED, and this entry takes those letters climbing back up the grid

explanation.surface: A nervous guest arrives at dinner with only the pudding on their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: STRESSED reversed is the neatest reversal in English, and 'turned up' pretends to mean arrived rather than telling you which way to read.
explanation.definitionFit: Desserts are the sweet courses at the end of a meal, matching the plural definition — the answer names the category those courses fall into.

clue.text: Out of hospital, frequently visit relative

indicators.note: 'Out of' is the removal instruction: the letter it names comes out of the longer word rather than being added to it.

parts.note: to haunt a place is to visit it again and again
H is the standard short form of hospital, as on a British road sign, and it is the letter taken out

explanation.surface: Now that you are out of hospital you can call on your relative as often as you like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of hospital' reads as being discharged, and that is the whole disguise: the same three words are an instruction to remove a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An aunt is a relative by blood or by marriage, so the definition is the plain category word — one relative, singular as the answer is.

clue.text: Extort from girlfriend?

definitions.meaning: the sense of putting the pressure on somebody until the money comes out
the informal noun for the person somebody is going out with, which the question mark marks as slang

explanation.surface: Somebody is putting the screws on the person they are seeing.
explanation.walkthrough: The slang sense is 1920s American and survives mainly in 'main squeeze', while the extortion sense is the same physical image put to work on a wallet.
explanation.definitionFit: To squeeze someone is to extort money from them; and your squeeze is the person you are going out with, which the question mark marks as informal.

clue.text: Hospital department entertained by youngster kept unwillingly

indicators.note: To entertain a guest is to have them inside your house, so the piece named first goes within the piece named after it.

parts.note: a pup is a young dog, and the word is used of other young creatures too
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a British hospital

explanation.surface: A small child is keeping the whole hospital department amused.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end and reads as more of the hospital scene, so the join falls between 'youngster' and 'kept' rather than anywhere the sentence suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Pent-up describes feelings or people shut in and not let out, which is what being kept somewhere unwillingly amounts to.

clue.text: He'll bring drink one assumes

indicators.note: 'assumes' is used in its take-on sense: the word takes the letter into itself instead of standing beside it.

parts.note: water is the drink that arrives without being ordered
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Presumably somebody will be along with the drinks before long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One assumes' reads as 'presumably', which is the whole disguise: both of its words are working, one as a letter and one as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A waiter is the one who brings your order to the table, so 'he'll bring' defines him by the job rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Team taking part in Whitechapel event

indicators.note: 'taking part in' asks for a part of the words that follow: the letters are inside them, not clued separately.

parts.note: the letters run consecutively over the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A team is entered for a sports day being held in Whitechapel.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitechapel is the East End district, and it is here purely to supply letters — no part of the answer has anything to do with the place.
explanation.definitionFit: A British cricket or football side is called an eleven, after the number of players, so 'team' is that everyday sporting sense.

clue.text: French writer appearing in European court to exit rapidly

indicators.note: 'appearing in' places the piece before it inside the letters named after it, showing up in the middle of them.

parts.note: E is the standard short form of European
ct is the abbreviation for court, the one used in street addresses
the writer of a clue is 'I', and the French for I is je

explanation.surface: A French novelist is making an appearance before a European court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' means the person who wrote the clue, so it stands for the first person — a convention worth owning, because any writer in a clue may turn out to be I or me.
explanation.definitionFit: To eject is to get out in a hurry — the word a pilot uses for leaving an aircraft — which is exiting rapidly by any measure.

clue.text: Vexed witness reported dangerous swimming conditions

parts.note: cross is the everyday word for annoyed

indicators.note: 'reported' means passed on by mouth, so the second piece is spelt the way you hear it rather than the way its own word is written.

parts.note: to witness something is to see it, and that word has a homophone spelt quite differently

explanation.surface: An irritated onlooker tells the lifeguards that the water is not safe to swim in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vexed witness' reads as one angry person and it is two separate pieces, the second of them heard rather than read.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross sea is water where two wave systems meet at an angle, throwing up unpredictable surf that drowns strong swimmers.

clue.text: Sport Dawson dominates

parts.note: RU is rugby union, the game's usual short form on a fixture list
Les Dawson supplies his first name

explanation.surface: A player called Dawson is head and shoulders above everyone else in his sport.
explanation.walkthrough: Les Dawson was a British comedian famous for deadpan mother-in-law jokes and deliberately terrible piano playing; the sportsman the surface suggests never existed.
explanation.definitionFit: A side that rules its league dominates it, so the verb matches the definition sense for sense and in the third person.

clue.text: Departed towards the end

definitions.meaning: the funeral sense, used of a person who has died
the clock sense, well on in the evening or the season

explanation.surface: Somebody slipped away shortly before the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Both readings are ordinary English, and the trap is that they join into a single sentence about leaving early, which is neither of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Late is the obituary word for someone who has died, and also the plain sense of being well on in the day.

clue.text: Broadcast exposed anger

indicators.note: an exposed word has lost its outer covering, so its first and last letters go

parts.note: a programme that has been broadcast has been aired

explanation.surface: A programme went out on air and laid bare someone's fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is a verb in the past tense here, giving AIRED; 'exposed' strips its A and D.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is a literary word for wrath or rage, a synonym of anger.

clue.text: River borders dilapidated retail and holiday accommodation

indicators.note: 'borders' is a verb here: to border something is to lie along its edges, so the river's letters sit at both ends of the rest.

parts.note: the Trent is one of England's big rivers, and it does not stay in one piece

indicators.note: 'dilapidated' describes something that has fallen apart, and a fallen-apart word is put back together in a new order.

parts.note: six letters of fodder, shuffled and dropped between the river's two halves

explanation.surface: The river runs past a row of shabby shops and somewhere for visitors to stay.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trent is a setter's first choice when five river letters are wanted, and 'borders' is the word that breaks it in two instead of leaving it whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A trailer tent is the folding canvas unit towed behind a car and pitched at a campsite, which is holiday accommodation of the cheapest sort.

clue.text: Republican with ego stops mingling to progress publication

indicators.note: 'mingling' is guests mixing at a party, and letters told to mingle end up standing in new company.

parts.note: R is the standard short form of Republican in American politics
eight letters of fodder, joined by the R to make nine

explanation.surface: A politician too full of himself has stopped mixing with the guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' looks like the verb the sentence needs and is fodder instead, which is what keeps the anagram out of sight until you count the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to press is to send an issue off for printing, the step that moves a publication from copy to printed pages.

clue.text: Marvellous old queen in pursuit of drink

indicators.note: 'in pursuit of' means chasing along behind, so the piece doing the chasing is written after the one it chases.

parts.note: to sup is to drink, in small mouthfuls
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the queen on the pillar boxes

explanation.surface: An elderly queen is on the hunt for something to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the crossword's standard queen, and 'old' now does real work: there has been a king since 2022, so the letters belong to the late Elizabeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Super is the everyday British intensifier for marvellous, the adjective you use about something that has thoroughly pleased you.
